newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Embattled Australian dlr survives tough week.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Embattled Australian dlr survives tough week.

text.p: The Australian dollar put in its steadiest performance in days Friday stirring hopes in die-hard bulls that its month-long decline had bottomed.

Despite threatening to surpass last week's 5-1/2 month low of US$0.7738 for much of the week the dollar actually ended with slight gains. Traders said the resilience of support had surprised and forced a short market to cover for the weekend.

Fresh weakness in the mark and a lull in the hype about a domestic rate cut also cushioned the currency, although they emphasised the technical picture remained ugly and sentiment favoured selling rallies for an eventual test of US$0.7680.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the currency had drifted off to US$0.7788/93 from an early US$0.7790/95 but was still up on Thursday's late US$0.7753/58.
Resistance was seen at US$0.7810 where a thick layer of offshore offers were thought to be waiting, while support was pegged at last week's US$0.7738 low.

It also firmed on most crosses and especially the mark after Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said record German unemployment proved the economy was in a grave position which the bank could not ignore. That was taken as a sign of rate cuts to come and both dollars took advantage.

The U.S. currency cleared 1.60 marks and triggered knock-out option demand, while the local dollar climbed to 1.2468/84 marks from 1.2363/35 late Thursday. On the yen it firmed to 91.19/29 from 90.60/70 on reports a Ministry of Finance official had conceded it was difficult to reverse the US$/yen uptrend.
The local unit lost ground to its Kiwi counterpart, however, after New Zealand consumer prices rose a stronger than expected 0.7 percent, taking inflation to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent.
The data eclipsed any thought of a policy easing and lifted the Kiwi to US$0.7089/96 from US$0.7036/42 late Thursday, while the AUD slipped to NZ$1.0971/89 from NZ$1.1021/40.

In contrast the risk in Australia is still of another policy easing, although the outlook had been confused by Thursday's admission from the Bureau of Statistics that a new method of compiling the data had meant employment had been underestimated by 6,000 to 9,000 a month since August.

The Reserve Bank partly justified its three cuts in interest rates last year as necessary for getting unemployment down, so news that jobs growth had not been as weak as thought may give the bank board pause when it meets next on February 4.
By then it will know how inflation performed in the December quarter -- consumer price data are due January 29.
If inflation slowed as many expected, it would provide the scope for an easing if the board felt one was needed.

Domestic data today were secondary in nature but provided some promising news on inflation. The manufacturing output prices up only 0.1 percent in November which brought annual growth back to 0.4 percent from 0.8 in October.
Private sector credit, meanwhile, rose a relatively modest 0.4 percent in November but housing lending was up a more healthy 0.9 percent.
The only major figures next week are merchandise imports for December on Monday. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
